Has the AI Boom Lost Its Momentum?

The AI boom has rewarded early investors handsomely, but the opportunity now looks considerably less straightforward. After months of enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence, investors are increasingly questioning whether the enormous spending behind the technology can generate adequate returns.

According to Reuters on November 19, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had lost nearly 30% since early October, even as estimates for major technology companies' capital expenditure remained largely unchanged. Barclays strategists noted that hyperscaler spending forecasts for next year had yet to be revised downward, suggesting that the market's retreat has outpaced changes in investment expectations.

However, the concerns extend beyond valuations. Rising financing costs, regulatory uncertainty, and potential restrictions on data center construction have complicated the outlook. As examined in our coverage of AI infrastructure opportunities and financing risks following CoreWeave's earnings, strong demand alone cannot eliminate the financial risks associated with rapid expansion.

Could the Selloff Offer a Second Opportunity?

Wall Street, however, remains remarkably optimistic. Reuters reported on November 18 that 83% of analyst ratings on key AI stocks were Strong Buy recommendations, despite mounting concerns over profitability and debt. Yet Bank of America's November fund manager survey revealed a contrasting picture: nearly 40% of respondents believed companies were overinvesting, while more than half anticipated at least one hyperscaler cutting capital expenditure within six months.

This divergence complicates the investment case. As explored in our earlier examination of oversold AI stocks with substantial analyst upside, falling share prices can widen implied returns without necessarily improving fundamentals. Meanwhile, our analysis of AI infrastructure stocks facing growing short-seller skepticism highlights another dimension of the risks accompanying that opportunity.

For investors who missed the initial rally, the correction may offer another entry point. Plot Twist: As CFO, Nvidia's Interim CEO Said "Over 99%" of Singapore Billings Were for U.S. Customers ©Mariia Demchenko from Getty Images and Billion Photos via Canva
Key Takeaways

NVIDIA fell 14% on Friday after Reuters reported that the SEC's probe of the chipmaker is examining possible accounting issues.

As CFO in August 2025, interim CEO Colette Kress said over 99% of data center compute revenue billed to Singapore was for U.S.-based customers.

A U.S.-based buyer can still ship chips anywhere. Prosecutors say a Super Micro Computer co-founder sent NVIDIA-powered servers on to China.

At 8.7x forward earnings, NVIDIA is priced for a trust problem that can't clear while Kress runs the company.

NVIDIA (NVDA:NASDAQ) fell 14% on Friday, its worst day since January 2025, after Reuters reported that the SEC's probe of the chipmaker is examining possible accounting issues.

On Nov. 17, the Financial Times reported that NVIDIA booked $104 billion of revenue, almost half its global sales, through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, the same year it stopped breaking Singapore out in its results. Southeast Asia is also where prosecutors say a co-founder of Super Micro Computer (SMCI:NASDAQ) sent NVIDIA-powered servers on to China.

On its August 2025 earnings call, the last time NVIDIA broke out Singapore, then-CFO Colette Kress said:

"Singapore revenue represented 22% of second quarter's billed revenue as customers have centralized their invoicing in Singapore. Over 99% of data center compute revenue billed to Singapore was for U.S.-based customers."

Kress became interim CEO this month, and she kept the CFO job.

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia's Analyst Ratings

The word Kress left out

Former SEC enforcement official John Reed Stark pointed out on X that NVIDIA's 10-Q for that quarter limited the 99% figure to export-controlled data center chips, a limit Kress left out on the call. The 10-Q never said what share of the Singapore billing those chips made up.

The generous reading is Kress's own: if U.S. cloud giants centralizing their invoicing in Singapore were the buyers, her figure holds.

But a U.S.-based buyer can still send chips anywhere. Super Micro is based in San Jose, and it reported preliminary sales of $19.9 billion for the September quarter, up from $5.0 billion a year earlier. If regulators start tracing where chips billed to Singapore ended up, I'd expect the U.S. server makers that buy them in bulk to face questions next, and Super Micro is the one with history here.

On its earnings call held on Nov. 3, 2026, for its fiscal 2027 first quarter ended Sept. 30, Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) announced a raised full-year revenue outlook. For long-term investors, accelerating server deployment schedules and expanding custom liquid-cooling infrastructure signal sustained market share gains in artificial intelligence hardware. Three things management said stand out.

1. Full-Year Revenue Guidance Rises on AI Demand

Management raised its fiscal 2027 revenue target. This revision reflects improving visibility into customer deployment schedules and sustained demand for high-performance server clusters.

We anticipate our fiscal 2027 revenue target will be in the range of $72 billion to $82 billion. That is about 12% higher than the target we set one quarter ago.
-- Charles Liang, Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer

2. Customer Prepayments Dramatically Improve Working Capital Efficiency

The cash conversion cycle, which measures how fast a business turns inventory investments back into cash, dropped by 52 days. Customer prepayments and faster manufacturing turnarounds funded most of the working capital needed to support rapid revenue scaling.

Our cash conversion cycle improved from 149 days to 97 days, a 52-day improvement in a single quarter. At our Q1 revenue run rate, that difference represents roughly $10 billion of working capital the business would otherwise have needed to fund.
-- Mark Long, Chief Financial Officer

3. System Building Blocks Drive Higher Profitability Across Accounts

Non-GAAP gross margin, which measures adjusted profit remaining after direct production costs without stock compensation expenses, expanded 3.3 percentage points year over year. Broader adoption of Data Center Building Block Solutions, or DCBBS, which provides modular hardware and management software, helped strengthen bottom-line performance.

We have executed our commitment to drive higher bottom line profitability in Q1. Non-GAAP gross margin expanded by 330 basis points year-over-year to 12.8%.
-- Charles Liang, Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer

Looking Ahead

Infrastructure build-outs continue to accelerate across major data center operators, and management isn't hiding its optimism about order momentum. Proprietary liquid-cooling integration, domestic manufacturing capacity, and flexible modular designs provide structural advantages that help customers deploy computing power faster. To gauge long-term execution, management is watching component availability and facility readiness to ensure customer sites can receive finished racks on schedule.

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Over the past five years, Dell stock has returned 447%. Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) has returned 220%. So $10,000 put in Dell five years ago is now worth about $54,700. The same amount in HPE is worth about $32,000. Dell and HP were once two similar hardware companies. What did Dell do differently? Was it one big decision, or many small ones?

Both stocks fell hard on Friday, Nov 20, as AI stocks sold off. Dell lost 11.0% and HPE 10.1%, while the S&P 500 fund (SPY) fell 3.6%. The returns below include that drop.

First, the gap. Dell beat HPE over one, three and five years. But HPE also beat the S&P 500 by a wide margin. The slow one is HP Inc, the PC half of the old HP. Over five years, $10,000 grew to about $10,600 in HP Inc. In the S&P 500 it grew to about $15,800.

Dell stock is up 447% in five years, and HPE 220%. After gains that big, a sharp drop can be hard to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018. It also pays about 3 times the S&P 500's dividend yield. See how it held up.

The Big Decision: Going Private, Then Buying EMC

In 2013 Michael Dell and Silver Lake took Dell private. That means they bought out the public shareholders, so the stock stopped trading. It took Dell out of reach of quarterly pressure over a shrinking PC business. Revenue had fallen from $62.1 billion in fiscal 2012 to $56.9 billion.

In 2016 Michael Dell closed the purchase of EMC, one of the largest tech deals ever. It made Dell a major storage company alongside its servers. Revenue went from $50.9 billion in fiscal 2016 to $78.7 billion two years later. Dell returned to the stock market in 2018. In 2021 it spun off VMware into a separate company. It used a $9.3 billion VMware dividend to pay down debt.

What Did HP Do Instead?

HP went the other way. In fiscal 2006 HP sold $91.7 billion, 1.6 times Dell's $55.8 billion. In 2015 its board split it into HP Inc and HPE. In 2017 HPE shed its services and software arms. Its revenue fell from $50.1 billion to $28.9 billion in a year. In 2025 HPE bought Juniper Networks.

Last fiscal year, Dell's sales of $113.5 billion topped both HP companies combined, at $89.6 billion. One company was rebuilt by its founder. The other was split up by its board.

Super Micro Computer Investment Narrative Recap

To own Super Micro Computer, you need to believe the AI infrastructure buildout supports sustained demand for its rack scale server, storage, and cooling platforms, even with structurally thinner margins and a volatile share price. According to RogueEP, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, this is a good stock in a tougher business, with value in disciplined assumptions rather than a smooth story.

Right now the key near term catalyst is execution on the huge AI focused revenue and rack capacity ambitions while managing funding that relies on higher risk borrowing and non cash heavy earnings. The biggest risk sits in any slowdown or pause in large AI data center deployments that could leave new capacity underutilized.

The most relevant update here is Super Micro Computer's launch of the H15 server portfolio and Petascale all flash storage platforms built around AMD's 6th Gen EPYC 9006 processors. Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

On profit, Dell stock looks cheap. Our earlier look at its earnings multiple found a stock priced for very little of its AI profit jump. At Thursday's close, it traded at 12.8 times the profit it expects to report this year.

A careful owner's next question is about cash. Profit is an accounting number. Free cash flow is the cash left after running and investing in the business. It pays down debt, buys back stock and pays dividends. Here we compare Dell's price with its cash now, over the last five years and three years out.

The short answer: at $313, Dell trades at 17.6 times its profit over the last four quarters. It trades at 23.4 times its free cash flow. Since early 2022, after the VMware spin-off, its middle cash multiple has been 16.2. On cash, Dell is not cheap today. It gets cheap only if the cash catches up with the profit.

Why Are Dell's Two Multiples So Far Apart?

AI servers take cash before they give it back. Dell buys Nvidia chips and builds the machines before customers pay. Its inventory doubled in six months, from $10.4 billion in January to $21.3 billion in July. Money owed by customers rose from $17.6 billion to $22.9 billion. In the first half of this fiscal year, Dell earned $7.6 billion but turned only $4.1 billion into free cash flow, 54 cents on the dollar. It still spent $6.0 billion on buybacks.

This gap swings both ways. Over its last four fiscal years, Dell's cash ran from 23% of its profit to 184% of it. It averaged about 100%. When orders slow, inventory turns back into cash. When orders surge, cash lags.

Dell's price today counts on $21.3 billion of inventory turning into cash. If Dell is a big share of your savings, you are counting on it too. The Trefis Income Solution fell less than the S&P 500 in each of the 9 big sell-offs since 2018, and it pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's. See how it held up.

How Does Today Compare With The Last Five Years?

On cash, Dell is pricier now than at most points since early 2022. Its cash multiple has ranged from 5.1 in January 2022 to above 50 in early 2023, when cash briefly dried up. Today's 23.4 sits above the middle of that range. Its profit multiple of 17.6 sits near the middle of its own range.

Although media reports or rumors about a significant change in a company's business prospects usually cause its stock to trend and lead to an immediate price change, there are always certain fundamental factors that ultimately drive the buy-and-hold decision.

Revisions to Earnings Estimates

Here at Zacks, we prioritize appraising the change in the projection of a company's future earnings over anything else. That's because we believe the present value of its future stream of earnings is what determines the fair value for its stock.

We essentially look at how sell-side analysts covering the stock are revising their earnings estimates to reflect the impact of the latest business trends. And if earnings estimates go up for a company, the fair value for its stock goes up. A higher fair value than the current market price drives investors' interest in buying the stock, leading to its price moving higher. This is why empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock price movements.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise reports its fiscal fourth quarter on Monday, Nov 23, after the market close. Can HPE's AI servers lift its margin, or only its sales? The short answer is mixed. So far, HPE's margin has risen along with its sales. But HPE credits ordinary servers and networking for that, not AI servers. HPE itself expects AI servers to pull the margin back down.

Gross margin is the share of sales left after the direct cost of making the products. HPE's gross margin was 40.1% in the three months to July. A year earlier it was 29.2%. Revenue grew 33.7% over the same year.

AI servers were a small part of that. HPE's AI Systems revenue was almost $1.6 billion in the quarter. That is less than 13.1% of its revenue. HPE said the margin came from "disciplined pricing in traditional servers and increased networking mix".

We expect most previews to focus on AI server orders. This article looks at one number instead, the gross margin.

Where does HPE stock stand before the report?

HPE closed at $45.49 on Thursday. That is 38.1% below its Oct 9 close of $73.46, its highest of the past year. On Thursday, the S&P 500 fell 2.02%. HPE slipped 0.63%.

HPE now sits 38.1% under its October high, and Monday's report can move it again. If HPE is a big part of your savings, that is a fall you may have to sit through. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record.

The other AI hardware names have fallen further from their peak closes of the past year:

Dell Technologies is 46.9% below its Sep 17 record close.

Super Micro Computer is 52.5% below its June 2 high.

Nvidia, which makes the chips inside these servers, is 39.0% below its Oct 6 record close.

Did HPE's margin rise because of AI servers?

Not by HPE's own account. Its gross margin bottomed at 28.4% in the quarter to April 2025. It then rose in each of the next five quarters, to 40.1%. That is the highest of the 11 quarters Morningstar returns.

It is also well above HPE's normal level. Its gross margin averaged 33.1% a year from fiscal 2021 to 2025.

The server unit grew, but on price, not AI. HPE's Cloud & AI unit had $9 billion of revenue. HPE said higher prices for ordinary servers drove server revenue to an all-time high. The unit's operating margin, the share of sales left after all running costs, was 17%.

What does HPE expect AI servers to do to its margin?

HPE expects the margin to come down. It said gross margin should "moderate toward more historical levels". It named two causes, growth in AI systems and ordinary server margins returning to normal. More networking should partly offset that.
